bib.title: SPREADSHEETLLM: Encoding Spreadsheets for Large Language Models

question: How can large, multi-table spreadsheets be serialized for LLMs within token limits while preserving the layout and structure needed for table detection and QA?
hypothesis: Most rows and columns in big spreadsheets are homogeneous and uninformative for layout, so dropping them and compacting the rest improves accuracy and cuts tokens.
contributions: SPREADSHEETLLM and SHEETCOMPRESSOR, an encoding framework that compresses spreadsheets for LLMs
Fine-tune several LLMs for spreadsheet table detection and show high accuracy
Chain of Spreadsheet (CoS) for downstream tasks, validated on spreadsheet QA

method.summary: Cells are serialized as address, value, format in a Markdown-like text. SheetCompressor then (1) keeps only rows/columns within k=4 of heuristically proposed structural anchors and re-maps coordinates, (2) inverts the index into {value: address/range} dropping empty cells, (3) replaces numeric cells with number-format strings or type tags and merges adjacent same-type cells into ranges. Chain of Spreadsheet runs table detection on the compressed sheet, then answers on the detected table re-encoded without extraction.
method.task: spreadsheet table detection and spreadsheet QA

datasets.name: TableSense spreadsheet table detection data (Dong et al., 2019b)
datasets.size: train 7000 items, valid 200 items, test 188 spreadsheets with 311 tables
datasets.split: test partitioned by vanilla token count: small <4k, medium 4-8k, large 8-32k, huge >32k, 64:32:70:22
datasets.source: real-world spreadsheets; test relabelled by five annotators (Fleiss Kappa 0.830 before cleaning)
datasets.preprocessing: Test: drop non-English sheets, drop sheets sharing a workbook with training, three-type annotation (167 sheets/268 tables type 1; 21/43 type 2; 10 type 3), types 1 and 2 kept = 188

datasets.name: Spreadsheet QA (new)
datasets.source: sampled from authors' collection; five annotators plus two cross-verifiers (Fleiss Kappa 0.846)
datasets.preprocessing: English only, no non-ASCII; questions limited to search, comparison, basic arithmetic; answer is a cell address or formula; 9 single-table, 35 two-table, 11 three-table, 9 four-plus-table sheets

models.name: GPT4 (fine-tuned and ICL, GPT4-0125-preview for ICL)

other.note: single-table QA baselines fed the detected table, truncated if over their limit

training.objective: fine-tuning on table boundary detection (output ranges like A2:D5)

other.gpt_finetune: lora_dim=32, n_epochs=-1, batch_size=-1, learning_rate_multiplier=1, weight_decay_multiplier=1e-05, prompt_loss_weight=0, trim_mode=right

inference.prompting: Instruction plus encoded spreadsheet; table detection one-shot instruction; QA is two-stage CoS (stage 1 compressed sheet -> table range; stage 2 uncompressed table -> cell address). Tables over 4096 tokens split with header repeated and 3 body rows per chunk (Algorithm 2).

parameters.data_types: Year, Integer, Float, Percentage, Scientific notation, Date, Time, Currency, Email, Others; first nine cover about 55% of cells

metrics.name: micro F1 under EoB-0
metrics.definition: Error-of-Boundary 0: predicted table must match top, left, bottom and right boundary exactly

metrics.name: compression ratio
metrics.definition: r = n/n', token count before over after

metrics.name: QA accuracy
metrics.definition: answer correct if cell address or cell combination/calculation is correct

metrics.name: cost
metrics.definition: ICL price proportional to input tokens, output ignored

eval.protocol: Single run per configuration apparently; no seeds, variance or significance reported.

results.claim: Inverted-index translation alone raises compression from 4.41 to 14.91 (with extraction); format aggregation raises it to 24.79.

results.claim: Structural-anchor extraction filters out 75% of spreadsheet content but keeps 97% of rows and columns at table edges (k=4).
results.quote: This method filters out 75% spreadsheet content but preserves 97% rows and columns at the edges of table boundaries.

results.claim: Anchor neighbourhood k=4 is best: F1 0.759 vs 0.712 (k=2) and 0.744 (k=8) on fine-tuned GPT4.
results.note: k=8 collapses on Huge (0.400) because of token limits.

limits: Cell formats (colour, borders, bold) are not used because they cost too many tokens and LLMs use them poorly (Limitations, App. A).
No semantic compression of natural-language cells (e.g. grouping countries as 'Country').
Anchor extraction is lossy; CoS re-encodes the detected table without extraction to recover detail.
Full pipeline slightly lowers F1 versus no aggregation (0.759 vs 0.789): aggregation trades accuracy for compression.
QA set is small (307 items), single-operation questions only; no repeated runs, seeds or significance tests; no code or data release stated in text.
Table 2 fine-tuned GPT4 row and ICL results use different GPT4 versions; GPT4 and baselines not run through the same budgets, and the QA baselines were truncated when over their limits.
Abstract headline 78.9% F1 is the variant without aggregation, not the 25x-compression pipeline.
